## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sālikedārajātaka* (Ja 484) is a Jātaka narrative set at Jetavana, delivered by the Buddha concerning a monk who supported his elderly mother and father [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1887]. Commending the monk for continuing the ancient lineage of the wise, the Buddha relates a story of the past opening with the verse *Sampannaṁ sālikedāraṁ*, recounting how he was once born as a parrot king (*suvarājā*) who gathered food in his beak to sustain his aged parents residing in their nest [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1887]. In the identification of the birth characters (*samodhāna*), the parrot flock corresponds to the Buddha's retinue, the parrot parents to the great royal families, the field-watcher (*khettapāla*) to Channa, the brahmin to Ānanda, and the parrot king to the Bodhisatta, with the dutiful monk attaining the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*) upon hearing the teaching [Fausböll 1887].

SuttaCentral records four translations across four languages [SuttaCentral]. In DharmaNexus, the text exhibits 22 Pali-internal matches (2,464 characters) with the commentary in the fourth volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (longest alignment §8.4–12.4 ↔ §2607–2619 with 0.93 similarity), while no cross-language parallels with a score of 10 or higher are recorded [DharmaNexus].
